/-!
# Erdős Problem 649

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/649](https://www.erdosproblems.com/649)
- [Ma35] Mahler, Kurt, *Über den grössten Primteiler spezieller Polynome zweiten Grades*. Archiv
  für math. og naturvid (1935).
- [Ro64b] Rotkiewicz, André, *Sur les nombres naturels $n$ et $k$ tels que les nombres $n$ et $nk$
  sont à la fois pseudopremiers*. Atti Accad. Naz. Lincei Rend. Cl. Sci. Fis. Mat. Nat. (8)
  (1964), 816-818.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos649

/--
Let $P(m)$ denote the greatest prime factor of $m$. Is it true that, for any two primes $p,q$,
there exists some integer $n$ such that $P(n)=p$ and $P(n+1)=q$?

In fact, the answer to this question as written is easily seen to be no, since there are no
solutions to $2^k\equiv -1\pmod{7}$, and hence this fails with $p=2$ and $q=7$. It is possible
that Erdős meant to exclude such obstructions, by amending this to 'odd primes' or 'all
sufficiently large primes' or such.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos649.lean"]
theorem erdos_649 : answer(False) ↔
    ∀ p q : ℕ, p.Prime → q.Prime →
      ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q := by
  sorry

/--
In fact, the answer to this question as written is easily seen to be no, since there are no
solutions to $2^k\equiv -1\pmod{7}$, and hence this fails with $p=2$ and $q=7$.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_649.variants.no_solution_two_seven :
    ¬ ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = 2 ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = 7 := by
  rintro ⟨n, hn, hn'⟩
  have h1n : 1 < n := by
    have := (Nat.one_lt_maxPrimeFac_iff n).mp (by omega)
    omega
  -- Since `2` is the greatest prime factor of `n`, it is the only one, so `n` is a power of `2`.
  obtain ⟨k, hpow⟩ : ∃ k, n = 2 ^ k :=
    ⟨_, Nat.eq_prime_pow_of_unique_prime_dvd (by omega)
      (fun {q} hq hqd ↦
        le_antisymm (hn ▸ Nat.le_maxPrimeFac (by omega) hq hqd) hq.two_le)⟩
  -- On the other hand `7` divides `n + 1`, i.e. `2 ^ k ≡ -1 (mod 7)`.
  have h7 : 7 ∣ n + 1 := hn' ▸ Nat.maxPrimeFac_dvd
  -- This is impossible: `2 ^ k` is congruent to `1`, `2` or `4` modulo `7`, never to `6`.
  have hmod : 2 ^ k % 7 = 2 ^ (k % 3) % 7 := by
    conv_lhs => rw [← Nat.div_add_mod k 3, pow_add, pow_mul]
    rw [Nat.mul_mod, Nat.pow_mod]
    norm_num
  have hk3 : k % 3 < 3 := Nat.mod_lt _ (by norm_num)
  interval_cases h : k % 3 <;> omega

/--
Even with such amendments, this problem is false in a strong sense: Alan Tong has provided the
following elegant elementary proof that, for any given prime $p$, there are infinitely many
primes $q$ such that this statement is false: let $m$ be the product of all primes $\leq p$, and
choose a prime $q$ congruent to $-1$ modulo $4m$. If $p$ is the greatest prime divisor of $n$
then, using quadratic reciprocity, every prime divisor of $n$ is a quadratic residue modulo $q$,
and hence $n$ is a quadratic residue modulo $q$. On the other hand, since $q\equiv 3\pmod{4}$ we
know that $-1$ is not a quadratic residue modulo $q$, and hence $n\not\equiv -1\pmod{q}$, so it
is impossible for $q\mid n+1$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_649.variants.tong (p : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) :
    {q : ℕ |
      q.Prime ∧ ¬ ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
Tong asks whether, for any given odd prime $q$, there are infinitely many primes $p$ such that
there is no integer $n$ with $P(n)=p$ and $P(n+1)=q$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_649.variants.tong_question : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ q : ℕ, q.Prime → Odd q →
      {p : ℕ |
        p.Prime ∧ ¬ ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
Sampaio independently observed that the answer to Erdős' original problem is no if one of the
primes can be $2$ - for example this is false with $p=19$ and $q=2$, since if $n+1=2^k$ and
$19\mid n$ then (since $2$ is a primitive root modulo $19$) we must have $18\mid k$, and hence
$73\mid 2^{18}-1\mid n$.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_649.variants.sampaio :
    ¬ ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = 19 ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = 2 := by
  sorry

/--
Problem 6 in the 12th Romanian Master of Mathematics Competitions in 2020 was to prove that there
exist infinitely many odd primes $p$ such that, for every $n$, $P(n)P(n+1)\neq 2p$.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_649.variants.rmm_2020 :
    {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ Odd p ∧
      ∀ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac * (n + 1).maxPrimeFac ≠ 2 * p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos649

findings.description: The right-hand side `∀ p q : ℕ, p.Prime → q.Prime → ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q` also ranges over equal primes, p = q. In that case no n can exist: p ∣ n and p ∣ n + 1 would give p ∣ 1, because gcd(n, n+1) = 1. So the right-hand side is false for a trivial reason, and `answer(False) ↔ …` holds without any of the source's mathematics. I checked this in Lean. A 5-line lemma `no_equal (p) (hp : p.Prime) : ¬ ∃ n, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n+1).maxPrimeFac = p` (proved from `Nat.maxPrimeFac_dvd` and `Nat.dvd_add_right`) is enough; the statement then follows as `⟨False.elim, fun h => no_equal 2 Nat.prime_two (h 2 2 Nat.prime_two Nat.prime_two)⟩`, which never mentions the (2, 7) obstruction. The source's question is about two distinct primes. Its negative answer rests on the pair p = 2, q = 7, the same argument the file's own docstring gives. The Lean statement therefore claims something weaker and trivial: that not every pair of possibly equal primes occurs, rather than that some pair of distinct primes does not occur. In the same way, if this were stated with `answer(sorry)`, the degenerate case would settle it trivially. This matches an earlier fix in this repository (Erdős 204, PR #2209): a missing `d ≠ d'` made a solved `answer(False)` statement trivially true, and it was labelled a misformalization.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/649 (read via its HTML/LaTeX views): "Is it true that, for any two primes $p,q$, there exists some integer $n$ such that $P(n)=p$ and $P(n+1)=q$?" … "Erdős writes 'it is probably hopelessly difficult to decide about the truth of this conjecture'." … "In fact, the answer to this question as written is easily seen to be no, since there are no solutions to $2^k\equiv -1\pmod{7}$, and hence this fails with $p=2$ and $q=7$." The source takes (2, 7) as the obstruction for the question 'as written', and Erdős calls it hopelessly difficult. Both only make sense if the two primes are distinct; with p = q allowed, the answer would be an immediate 'no'.
findings.suggested_fix: Add distinctness: `theorem erdos_649 : answer(False) ↔ ∀ p q : ℕ, p.Prime → q.Prime → p ≠ q → ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q`. Optionally say in the docstring that p ≠ q is needed because P(n) = P(n+1) is impossible. I checked that the corrected statement is proved by `⟨False.elim, fun h => erdos_649.variants.no_solution_two_seven (h 2 7 Nat.prime_two (by norm_num) (by norm_num))⟩`.

reformulations.difference: The Lean quantifies over every `n : ℕ`, so it includes the junk values `maxPrimeFac 0 = 0` and `maxPrimeFac 1 = 1`, and uses the product form `P(n)·P(n+1) ≠ 2p`. The competition problem (official RMM 2020 P6) says n > 1 and speaks of unordered pairs {gpf(n), gpf(n+1)}.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For n = 0 and n = 1 the products are 0·1 = 0 and 1·2 = 2, and 2p ≥ 6 for an odd prime p, so these values never matter. For n > 1 both greatest prime factors are prime, so by unique factorization their product equals 2p exactly when {P(n), P(n+1)} = {2, p}. I proved in Lean that `(∀ n : ℕ, …) ↔ (∀ n, 1 < n → …)`. The product form is also the one the cited site uses.

could_not_verify: Erdos649.erdos_649: I could not get Erdős's original wording in [Er95c]; the Rényi Institute archive index stops at 1989 and the site's bibliography loads dynamically. So the reading of 'two primes' as distinct rests on the erdosproblems.com text and commentary: its (2, 7) discussion of the question 'as written', and its quote of Erdős calling the question 'hopelessly difficult'. Whether maintainers treat a trivialized but still-true solved statement as a misformalization is a matter of judgment, though precedents #2209 and #1903 suggest they do. Hence confidence 0.6.
review.notes:
I checked all six declarations: `erdos_649`, `no_solution_two_seven`, `tong`, `tong_question`, `sampaio` and `rmm_2020`. Only `erdos_649` has a defect: it has no p ≠ q hypothesis.

- **Domain of n.** The source's 'integer n' is formalised as `n : ℕ`, and that is the right reading. Witnesses must have n ≥ 2 anyway, because `maxPrimeFac 0 = 0` and `maxPrimeFac 1 = 1` are not prime; I proved this in Lean. The source cannot mean all of ℤ: n = −8 gives (P(n), P(n+1)) = (2, 7), so the site's (2, 7) obstruction and Tong's quadratic-residue argument both assume n > 0.
- **Orientation checks.** `#eval` shows (2, 19) occurs (n = 512) and (7, 2) occurs (n = 7). So the order of the pairs in `sampaio` (19, 2) and `no_solution_two_seven` (2, 7) matters, and both match the site. I also confirmed that 2^18 − 1 = 3^3·7·19·73 and that the order of 2 mod 19 is 18.
- **Tong's variants.** In `tong` and `tong_question`, the degenerate element q = p (or p = q) is in the set trivially, but a single element cannot change whether the set is infinite. Both statements are faithful. `tong_question` puts the source's affirmative question in the `answer(sorry)` slot with the correct scope, and it is still recorded as open ('Tong's question (no answer)' on the forum).
- **`rmm_2020`.** It follows the site's paraphrase. The official RMM 2020 P6 (proposed by Krachun) only asks for infinitely many strange unordered pairs of distinct primes, with n > 1. The official solution proves this with pairs {2, q}, which is exactly the stronger form the site and the Lean state. So the statement is true and faithful to the cited source; the linked proof repository also proves it.
- **Status.** Everything is consistent with the source. The site says 'DISPROVED (LEAN)', and the `formal_proof` URL resolves to a proof of `¬ ∀ p q prime, ∃ n, P n = p ∧ P (n+1) = q` via (2, 7). Its `P` differs from `maxPrimeFac` only at 1, which cannot matter here. `tong` is solved (the site gives the proof), the other variants are elementary, and `tong_question` is open.
- **After the fix.** The linked external proof also has no p ≠ q, but it uses (2, 7), so it adapts directly. Once p ≠ q is added, the file's own `no_solution_two_seven` proves the corrected `erdos_649` in one line; I checked this.

demonstrated.claim: The theorem `erdos_649_from_p_eq_q : type_of% @Erdos649.erdos_649` proves the declaration exactly as stated in 5 lines, using only the degenerate pair p = q = 2 (no n has maxPrimeFac n = 2 = maxPrimeFac (n+1), because 2 ∣ n and 2 ∣ n + 1, which omega refutes) and never the source's (2, 7) obstruction; the missing `p ≠ q` makes the right-hand side trivially false.

submission.summary: `/workspace/review/trivial_proof.lean` imports `FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«649»` and names the declaration's type directly with `type_of% @Erdos649.erdos_649`. The `#check` line shows that type: `False ↔ ∀ p q : ℕ, p.Prime → q.Prime → ∃ n, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q`. The file proves it in five tactic lines. It instantiates the right-hand side at p = q = 2, turns the two `maxPrimeFac` equalities into 2 ∣ n and 2 ∣ n + 1 using `Nat.maxPrimeFac_dvd`, and closes the goal with `omega`. The proof never uses the 2^k ≢ −1 (mod 7) argument that the source and the file's own docstring give for the negative answer. That shows the statement is settled by the degenerate case alone, because the hypothesis `p ≠ q` is missing. The file compiles with no errors, no warnings and no `sorry`. `#print axioms` lists only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. Nothing under /opt/formal-conjectures was modified; the existing `lakefile.toml` change and `run/` directory predate this session.

trivial_proof.lean:
import FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«649»

/-!
Trivial proof of `Erdos649.erdos_649` as stated: it is settled by the degenerate case `p = q`.
-/

#check @Erdos649.erdos_649

-- Erdos649.erdos_649: provable from the degenerate case p = q = 2 alone (no n has
-- P(n) = P(n+1) = 2, since 2 ∣ n and 2 ∣ n + 1), without the source's (2, 7) obstruction:
-- the statement lacks `p ≠ q`, so its right-hand side is trivially false.
theorem erdos_649_from_p_eq_q : type_of% @Erdos649.erdos_649 := by
  refine ⟨False.elim, fun h => ?_⟩
  obtain ⟨n, h1, h2⟩ := h 2 2 Nat.prime_two Nat.prime_two
  have : 2 ∣ n := h1 ▸ Nat.maxPrimeFac_dvd
  have : 2 ∣ n + 1 := h2 ▸ Nat.maxPrimeFac_dvd
  omega

#print axioms erdos_649_from_p_eq_q

submission.summary:
I fixed `Erdos649.erdos_649` by adding `p ≠ q →` to its right-hand side. It now reads `answer(False) ↔ ∀ p q : ℕ, p.Prime → q.Prime → p ≠ q → ∃ n : ℕ, n.maxPrimeFac = p ∧ (n + 1).maxPrimeFac = q`. Before, the case p = q made the statement trivially provable: P(n) = P(n+1) is impossible because n and n+1 are coprime. Now the negative answer depends on the source's (2, 7) obstruction. I added one docstring sentence explaining why p and q must be distinct, following the AGENTS.md rule for restrictions that exclude a degenerate case.

I kept `research solved`, `AMS 11`, `answer(False)` and the `formal_proof` link. The linked Lean proof disproves the claim with p = 2 and q = 7, which are distinct, so it covers the corrected statement, although its theorem is itself written without `p ≠ q`.

In a scratch file I checked that:
- a verbatim copy of the corrected statement follows in one line from the file's already-proved `erdos_649.variants.no_solution_two_seven`;
- the corrected statement implies the old one, so it is strictly stronger.

No other declaration was changed. The edited file compiles with only the five `declaration uses 'sorry'` warnings the original already had. Nothing else under /opt/formal-conjectures was changed by me: the `lakefile.toml` edit and the `run/` directory were already there when I started.
